critique: Seeing a shape, imagining it, and thinking about it may represent the same object and properties while feeling very different. Representational content alone therefore appears insufficient to fix phenomenal character.

label: Mood and bodily sensation resist world-directed content
critique: Diffuse anxiety, pain, and undirected moods have distinctive phenomenal character without clearly representing external objects as having properties. Expanding content to include bodily or evaluative representation risks becoming ad hoc.

label: Transparency does not prove identity
critique: The fact that attention naturally goes to represented features may show only that introspection is limited or outwardly directed. It does not establish that phenomenal qualities are nothing over and above representational content.

label: Misrepresentation cases are underdetermined
critique: Hallucinations can feel exactly like veridical perceptions despite representing no actual object. The theory must explain what fixes their content without relying on the phenomenal character it is meant to explain.

label: An illusion still seems to require appearance
critique: For an illusion of phenomenal properties to occur, there must be some way the mental state appears to the subject. Denying all qualitative appearance makes it unclear what distinguishes the alleged illusion from a merely verbal false belief.

label: Reports may be direct evidence, not a target for deflation
critique: First-person judgments about pain and color experience are among the data a theory of mind should explain, not automatically reinterpret as error. Illusionism discounts the evidence because it conflicts with its ontology.

label: Functional duplication does not settle phenomenology
critique: Explaining why a system reports qualia does not show that the reports are false. A theory can account for the causal production of accurate testimony without reducing its subject matter to the reporting mechanism.

label: The view may preserve qualia under another name
critique: If the introspective representation has a distinctive subjective character that generates judgments, that character appears to play the role of the qualia illusionism rejects. The ontology may be redescribed rather than eliminated.

label: Functional parity ignores causal intimacy
critique: Biological memory is continuously integrated, automatically updated, and available without perception or deliberate action. A notebook may be reliable yet remain an instrument used by cognition rather than a constituent of it.

label: Coupling leads to cognitive bloat
critique: If reliable interaction is sufficient for constitution, phones, libraries, experts, and internet services may all become literal parts of a person’s mind. The theory needs a principled boundary that does not merely track intuitive cases.

label: Ownership and access can be interrupted
critique: External resources can be stolen, altered, or accessed by others without changing the person’s internal cognitive organization. Their independent vulnerability suggests they are environmental supports rather than parts of the subject.

label: Equivalent contribution does not imply constitutive identity
critique: Two components can make the same functional contribution while differing in whether they constitute the system or causally assist it. Parity of role underdetermines the metaphysical relation between agent and tool.

label: Branching defeats one-to-one identity
critique: If one psychology is copied into two future bodies, each successor can be equally continuous with the original. Numerical identity cannot hold between one earlier person and two later people, so continuity alone is insufficient.

label: Psychological continuity presupposes ownership
critique: A later memory counts as a genuine memory rather than a merely accurate apparent memory partly because it derives from the subject’s own earlier experience. Using memory to define identity therefore risks presupposing the identity relation.

label: Temporary unconsciousness creates gaps
critique: Coma, dreamless sleep, and severe amnesia can interrupt many psychological connections while the person plausibly survives. The theory needs an account of indirect continuity robust enough not to make persistence depend on accidental chains of mental access.

label: Embodied traits shape psychology
critique: Character, emotion, and agency depend on bodily systems and social recognition. Treating matter as replaceable underestimates how bodily continuity partly constitutes the very psychology taken as fundamental.

label: Brain transplant intuitions favor the mind
critique: If a person’s functioning brain were transplanted into another body, many would expect the person to go with the brain rather than remain with the emptied organism. This suggests that whole-body continuity is not decisive.

label: Legal practice is revisionary evidence
critique: Institutions track bodies largely because bodies are normally reliable proxies for minds and are easy to identify. Practical convention does not establish the metaphysical criterion in abnormal cases where those features diverge.

label: Body boundaries and replacement are vague
critique: Human bodies exchange matter continuously and can incorporate prostheses or transplanted organs. The account needs a principled biological continuity relation rather than appealing to an intuitively “same” body.

label: The view underexplains special concern
critique: People care about future experiences because they expect a continuation of consciousness, memory, and projects. Bare bodily persistence without psychological life does not seem to preserve the object of prudential concern.

label: The thinking-parts problem remains
critique: If the whole animal thinks, its brain or sufficiently large thinking part may also satisfy the same causal conditions for thought. Animalism needs a reason only the organism is the subject rather than one thinker among overlapping candidates.

label: Cerebrum transfer threatens organism tracking
critique: Transferring the structures supporting memory and agency to another organism would seem to move the person’s perspective and projects. Animalism says the original person remains with the largely mindless animal, which conflicts with strong survival intuitions.

label: Prenatal numerical identity is not obvious
critique: The fact that one organism develops continuously into an adult does not establish that a person already exists before any mental capacity. “Person” may designate a later phase or status rather than the animal simpliciter.

label: Unified biology does not settle normative identity
critique: Even if we are animals biologically, questions about responsibility, anticipation, and compensation may track psychological continuity. The metaphysical category of organism may not answer every practical question associated with personal identity.

label: Which brain parts matter is indeterminate
critique: Different neural systems support memory, affect, homeostasis, and agency, and these can be separated or replaced gradually. The view lacks a principled threshold specifying how much and which organization must persist.

label: Functional replacement challenges material continuity
critique: If neurons were gradually replaced by functionally equivalent devices, psychological life might continue despite the loss of the original brain matter. A material brain criterion would imply death where experience appears uninterrupted.

label: The brain is bodily, not an alternative to body
critique: Saying the person follows the brain selects one organ within the organism but does not explain why that organ alone constitutes the person. Its importance may derive from preserving psychology, making the theory derivative of psychological continuity.

label: Split-brain cases create multiple candidates
critique: If hemispheres can support partially independent centers of consciousness, a later division could produce two successors with comparable neural continuity. The brain criterion then inherits the one-to-many problem it was meant to avoid.

label: Non-narrative persons still persist
critique: Infants, people with severe cognitive impairments, and adults who do not organize life narratively remain persons over time. Narrative capacity may enrich agency without constituting basic identity.

label: Coherent stories can be false
critique: A person can sustain a highly coherent but confabulated self-story. If narrative coherence constitutes identity, distortion may count as successful selfhood even when it severs contact with actual history.

label: Multiple narratives can fit one life
critique: The same events can support incompatible stories of victimhood, growth, betrayal, or continuity. Without criteria for privileging one interpretation, narrative identity becomes unstable and potentially manipulable.

label: Constitution is confused with self-understanding
critique: A narrative can explain how someone understands and evaluates their life without determining whether the person is numerically identical across time. The argument moves from practical identity to metaphysical persistence.

label: Indexical anticipation seems left over
critique: Even with all continuity facts specified, a person facing duplication may still ask which future perspective they will experience. Reductionism labels the question empty without explaining why first-person anticipation appears to demand an answer.

label: Reduction does not choose among relations
critique: Physical and psychological continuities can diverge, branch, or hold by degrees. Saying identity reduces to “such relations” does not determine which pattern is sufficient for one persisting person.

label: Legal and moral practices require categorical decisions
critique: Responsibility, inheritance, and consent often require a yes-or-no subject. Gradual continuity facts may inform these decisions, but reductionism alone does not explain how categorical statuses should be assigned.

label: Supervenience is weaker than reduction
critique: If identity cannot vary without underlying facts varying, it supervenes on them. That does not show that identity claims are analyzable or eliminable in their terms, so the conclusion outruns the premise.

label: Extrinsic duplication changes identity retroactively
critique: One successor would count as the original if no copy were made, yet cease to be the original merely because a second copy exists elsewhere. Identity should not depend on an extrinsic event that changes nothing about the first successor.

label: Arbitrary asymmetry creates abrupt identity
critique: If two successors are nearly equal but one has a tiny advantage in continuity, the rule may assign identity entirely to that one. A minuscule difference then produces a categorical metaphysical discontinuity.

label: Uniqueness may be epistemically inaccessible
critique: A successor may not know whether a duplicate exists and therefore cannot know whether they are the original person. The account makes first-person identity depend on potentially hidden facts with no experiential impact.

label: The clause saves logic by abandoning sufficiency
critique: Branching shows that psychological continuity is not itself identity. Adding uniqueness prevents contradiction but does not explain why non-branching continuity suddenly becomes numerical identity rather than merely a close relation.

label: Memory presupposes identity
critique: A mental image counts as remembering an experience only if it is appropriately connected to an experience of the same subject. Otherwise it is merely an apparent or inherited memory, so memory cannot non-circularly define identity.

label: Identity is transitive while memory is not
critique: An elderly person may remember middle age, and the middle-aged person remember childhood, while the elderly person no longer remembers childhood. Identity remains transitive despite the failure of direct memory connection.

label: Amnesia would destroy persons too readily
critique: People can lose autobiographical memory through injury while retaining continuity of body, character, and social relations. It is implausible that ordinary amnesia creates a numerically new person.

label: False memory can mimic the criterion
critique: A perfectly implanted memory could feel first-personal and guide responsibility exactly like a genuine one. The theory needs causal provenance conditions that move the criterion beyond memory content itself.

label: Soul continuity is epistemically inaccessible
critique: Two souls could switch bodies or be replaced between moments without any observable or psychological difference. If no evidence can distinguish these possibilities, the soul criterion does not improve practical reidentification.

label: Simplicity does not guarantee persistence
critique: An entity’s lacking parts does not entail that it cannot cease to exist and be replaced by an exactly similar entity. The argument needs a persistence principle for souls, not merely their alleged simplicity.

label: Interaction with the brain is unexplained
critique: Changes to neural tissue systematically alter memory, personality, and consciousness. A soul theory must explain why an immaterial subject’s capacities track physical organization so closely without becoming causally redundant.

label: The posit duplicates explanatory work
critique: Psychological and biological continuities already account for observable persistence judgments. Adding an unobservable bearer that makes no independent predictions increases ontology without resolving which future psychology belongs to it.

label: Concern cannot be divided without dilution
critique: If two successors each receive only part of the original’s assets or opportunities, the original may care whether one or both are literally them. Psychological continuity alone does not determine how self-interested value should aggregate across branches.

label: Responsibility may require a single bearer
critique: Punishment and promise enforcement presuppose that a later subject is accountable for one earlier agent’s action. Extending full responsibility to every psychological continuer can multiply liability implausibly.

label: The view relies on contested intuitions about duplication
critique: Some people regard perfect copying as death followed by replacement, regardless of continuity. The argument assumes rather than establishes that preserved memories and projects capture the object of survival concern.

label: Numerical identity may explain why continuity matters
critique: Psychological continuity may matter because it is normally evidence of personal identity. In abnormal cases where they diverge, the derivative relation may lose the prudential significance borrowed from identity.

label: Agent causation is explanatorily opaque
critique: Saying that the agent causes the action without an event determining the choice does not explain why this action occurs rather than another. The view names a special causal relation where an account of control is needed.

label: Reasons either determine or fail to explain
critique: If the agent’s reasons sufficiently explain the choice, the outcome appears determined by them; if they do not, the residual selection seems arbitrary. Agent causation does not clearly escape this control-versus-randomness dilemma.

label: Substance causation conflicts with ordinary causal models
critique: Causal explanations ordinarily relate events or state changes with temporal structure. A persisting substance causing an event without a causally sufficient state is difficult to integrate with any general account of causation.

label: Ultimate sourcehood may be unnecessary
critique: Responsibility may require acting from one’s values and capacities, not being an uncaused origin. Demanding ultimate sourcehood sets a metaphysical standard stronger than ordinary practices of agency need.

label: Manipulated mechanisms can remain responsive
critique: An intervener could implant a values-and-deliberation system that responds sensitively to reasons while ensuring a desired action. The agent would meet the functional criterion yet seem controlled rather than free.

label: Suitable ranges are underdetermined
critique: Almost any mechanism responds to some reasons in some counterfactual situations. The theory needs a non-arbitrary standard for how broad, regular, and normatively appropriate the response pattern must be.

label: Recognition can be bypassed in actual action
critique: A mechanism may be generally reasons-responsive even though the present action results from compulsion or a malfunction. Counterfactual capacity does not guarantee that the agent exercised self-governance in the actual sequence.

label: Normative competence does not settle alternatives
critique: Reasons-responsiveness explains rational agency, but critics of determinism ask whether the agent could genuinely have chosen otherwise or authored their values. The account may change the subject rather than answer that concern.

label: Control is not closed under consequence
critique: A person can control an outcome even though it follows from background conditions they do not control, provided their own deliberation is among the sufficient conditions. Lack of control over premises does not automatically transfer to every consequence.

label: The past includes the agent’s forming dispositions
critique: Remote history may causally produce the agent, but present action can still flow through their values and reasoning. The argument treats causal ancestry as external constraint even when it constitutes the agent’s own capacities.

label: Ability can be conditional
critique: To say the agent could have acted otherwise may mean they would have done so if they had chosen or judged differently. Determinism is compatible with these conditionals, so the argument relies on a stronger and contested notion of control.

label: Natural laws do not compel as agents do
critique: Laws describe regularities or necessities connecting events; they are not forces that bypass deliberation. Framing actions as unavoidable “consequences” can suggest coercion where the causal route runs through ordinary agency.

label: A flicker of freedom may remain
critique: Before the controller’s intervention threshold, the agent may still be able to form a different intention, attend to another reason, or begin an alternative sequence. These residual possibilities could be what grounds responsibility.

label: The controller cannot guarantee without prior determination
critique: To know when to intervene infallibly, the controller needs a prior sign that either already determines the choice or leaves some alternative open. Frankfurt cases may therefore presuppose determinism or fail to remove alternatives.

label: Omission of intervention may still shape the modal context
critique: The agent acts in an environment engineered to eliminate successful alternatives. Intuitions of responsibility may track the actual internal process while overlooking that genuine freedom includes more than noninterference in the actual sequence.

label: Responsibility judgments may be partial
critique: The agent may deserve blame for their reasons or intention while not being fully responsible for the unavoidable outcome. The case does not establish that alternative possibilities are irrelevant to every dimension of responsibility.

label: Ordinary development includes authorship opportunities
critique: Normal agents gradually reflect on, resist, and revise influences through social interaction. Covert programming bypasses those diachronic capacities, so the histories differ in a way directly relevant to ownership of values.

label: Manipulation intuitions may track wrongdoing by manipulators
critique: The scenario includes deception and intentional control by another person, which elicit judgments of victimization. Those reactions do not show that impersonal deterministic causation removes freedom.

label: Similarity is too coarse
critique: Both histories are causal, but causal processes can differ in whether they preserve reasons, feedback, and self-correction. Calling them different only in complexity assumes that these structural distinctions are irrelevant.

label: The argument threatens libertarian agents too
critique: A manipulator could shape background desires while leaving a later indeterministic choice. If that agent also seems unfree, the problem concerns historical authenticity rather than determinism specifically.

label: Basic desert may not require ultimacy
critique: Responsibility can plausibly arise from acting knowingly through one’s evaluative capacities, even if those capacities have causes. The demand to be the ultimate origin of oneself is stronger than the concept of desert ordinarily implies.

label: Indeterminism can operate within agency
critique: An undetermined choice need not be external luck if it is resolved through the agent’s reasons and effort. The argument assumes that every non-determined contribution is merely random.

label: Forward-looking practices may reintroduce blame
critique: Censure and moral influence often express judgments that the wrongdoer is accountable, not merely a dangerous mechanism to be managed. Eliminating desert may alter these practices more radically than the position acknowledges.

label: Skepticism about desert is self-insulating
critique: Any ordinary example of responsibility can be dismissed because the agent did not create their own character. The view needs independent evidence that ultimacy is conceptually required rather than using that requirement to predetermine every case.

label: Owned values can be coercively installed
critique: A person may wholeheartedly endorse values implanted through manipulation and act from them without internal conflict. Present sourcehood then appears satisfied despite a history that undermines ownership.

label: No alternative can weaken rational control
critique: Responding to reasons seems to involve the capacity to change course when sufficient reasons arise. If the agent could not do otherwise under any relevant conditions, the attribution of rational control becomes thin.

label: Ownness is defined through the disputed freedom
critique: Calling values genuinely “the agent’s own” may already imply that they were acquired or maintained freely. Sourcehood cannot analyze freedom if its central ownership relation presupposes freedom.

label: Outcome responsibility may depend on avoidability
critique: An action can express character while an unavoidable harmful outcome remains less blameworthy. Sourcehood may ground attributability without replacing the role of alternatives in full moral responsibility.

label: Negligence can be culpable without occurrent awareness
critique: A driver who carelessly fails to check a blind spot may not consciously represent the resulting risk at the moment of harm. Responsibility can arise from a prior duty to cultivate attention, not only from present conscious control.

label: Skilled action is often automatic
critique: Experts perform complex actions through trained processes that are not consciously monitored step by step. Their automaticity can enhance rather than diminish agency and accountability.

label: Conscious awareness may be post hoc
critique: If conscious intentions partly report decisions initiated by unconscious processes, requiring consciousness as the causal governor may exclude ordinary intentional action. The position needs a less demanding relation between awareness and control.

label: Responsibility can attach to character expression
critique: Spontaneous cruelty or generosity may reveal stable values precisely because it is uncalculated. Moral appraisal often targets what an automatic response expresses about the person, not just deliberate governance.

label: Deviant causal chains defeat sufficiency
critique: An intention can cause nervousness, which accidentally produces the intended result, without the result being performed intentionally. Causation by intention is insufficient unless “the right way” is independently explained.

label: Some actions are omissions or mental acts
critique: Intentionally refraining, calculating silently, or deciding need not involve a bodily movement of the relevant kind. The proposed ontology is too narrow for the range of actions.

label: Basic actions may lack prior intentions
critique: A person can wave, speak, or catch an object spontaneously without forming a distinct intention that causes the movement. Treating every action as plan execution imposes an unnecessary temporal layer.

label: Intentions can be constitutive rather than causal
critique: The relation between intention and action may be one of rational organization or description, not event causation. Separating them into cause and effect can misrepresent intentional movement as two independent occurrences.

label: Apparent akrasia may involve judgment revision
critique: At the moment of action, the person may shift from an all-things-considered judgment to a narrower assessment emphasizing immediate reward. The behavior then follows the operative judgment rather than contradicting it.

label: All-things-considered judgments may be noncommittal
critique: A person can believe one option is best impersonally while preferring another for themselves. Without specifying the practical authority of the judgment, the alleged motivational gap may be semantic.

label: Compulsion cases are not freely akratic
critique: Addiction and entrenched habit can impair control rather than illustrate a free choice against judgment. The theory must distinguish weakness of will from inability, which many central examples blur.

label: The gap does not explain the action
critique: Stating that judgment failed to motivate identifies a mismatch but not the mechanism that allowed a weaker reason to prevail. A theory of akrasia needs an account of attention, desire, or temporal discounting.

label: Justice can be sacrificed for aggregate gain
critique: If punishing an innocent person would prevent riots and increase total welfare, the theory can require the punishment. Treating one person’s basic interests as fully exchangeable for others’ benefits fails to respect separateness of persons.

label: Demands can become unbounded
critique: Whenever resources spent on personal projects could produce more welfare elsewhere, ordinary discretionary spending appears wrong. The view leaves little principled space for partial commitments, rest, or a life organized around one’s own relationships.

label: Outcome calculation is epistemically infeasible
critique: Actions have diffuse long-term effects and uncertain interactions that agents cannot compare comprehensively. A criterion that routinely outruns human evidence may not provide the practical guidance its unity promises.

label: Well-being aggregation assumes interpersonal comparability
critique: The theory requires cardinal comparisons of gains and losses across people, yet there is no uncontested scale for doing so. Without that structure, the maximizing instruction is indeterminate.

label: Rules either collapse or become irrationally rigid
critique: If rules allow exceptions whenever breaking them increases welfare, the view collapses into act utilitarianism. If they forbid such exceptions, they can require avoidable harm solely to preserve a rule whose rationale is consequentialist.

label: The relevant level of rule specificity is arbitrary
critique: A broad rule may underperform while a highly qualified rule tailored to circumstances does better. Without a principled limit on complexity, the optimal rule can encode act-by-act maximization in disguised form.

label: Acceptance conditions vary across societies
critique: The welfare effects of a rule depend on institutions, expectations, and existing norms. The account may yield different moral rules for similarly situated individuals merely because their societies have different histories.

label: Ideal-code evaluation neglects transition costs
critique: A rule set may be optimal under universal acceptance but disastrous to introduce gradually in a noncompliant world. The theory needs guidance for actual agents facing partial adoption rather than only ideal equilibrium.

label: Maxim description determines the verdict
critique: The same action can be described by a broad maxim that fails universalization or a narrow maxim that passes. Without a non-arbitrary rule for formulating maxims, agents can engineer the test to support preferred conduct.

label: Unusual preferences yield perverse permissions
critique: An agent who welcomes a harsh universal practice may rationally will it even when it gravely harms others. Coherence with one’s will does not ensure adequate concern for welfare or rights.

label: Universal practice effects reintroduce consequences
critique: Many contradictions arise because universal adoption would frustrate an institution or goal, such as promising. The test then relies on predicted social consequences despite claiming to ground morality independently of them.

label: Consistency is too weak for substantive morality
critique: A coherent egoist can endorse universal principles that protect only those with certain powers or statuses. Rational consistency alone does not generate equal moral standing without an additional normative premise.

label: Reasonableness imports the moral verdict
critique: Whether a rejection is reasonable depends on which interests, burdens, and claims deserve priority. Those judgments are already substantive moral judgments, so the contractualist formula may organize rather than ground morality.

label: Numbers problem remains
critique: If one principle burdens one person severely while another burdens millions slightly, person-by-person rejection does not clearly explain when numerous small claims outweigh one large claim. Refusing aggregation can produce insensitive choices.

label: Nonparticipants are difficult to include
critique: Infants, cognitively impaired humans, future people, and animals cannot literally assess or reject principles. Representing their standpoints requires external judgments that weaken the agreement-based foundation.

label: Informed agreement may idealize away identity
critique: What people would reject under full information and freedom can differ sharply from their actual values. The account risks replacing justification to real persons with endorsement by constructed ideal agents.

label: The virtuous-agent standard is circular
critique: A good person is identified by acting rightly, while right action is identified by what a good person would do. Without an independent account of virtue or flourishing, the theory cannot break this circle.

label: Virtues can conflict without a decision rule
critique: Compassion may favor mercy while justice favors punishment, and loyalty may conflict with honesty. Invoking practical wisdom names the capacity to resolve conflict but does not explain which consideration should prevail.

label: Character focus can obscure institutions
critique: Systemic injustice can persist even when individuals display admirable traits within their roles. Moral analysis also needs principles for designing rules and allocating power, which agent-centered virtue language may underprovide.

label: Cultural variation challenges virtue lists
critique: Communities disagree about traits such as obedience, pride, modesty, and martial courage. The theory needs a standard for distinguishing genuine virtues from locally admired dispositions.

label: Context sensitivity does not eliminate principles
critique: A principle can include defeaters, enabling conditions, and role-sensitive clauses. The fact that one feature changes significance across cases shows that simple principles fail, not that no general structure governs reasons.

label: Learning and criticism require generalization
critique: Agents improve moral judgment by identifying recurring patterns and explaining why cases differ. Without general standards, it becomes difficult to teach, justify, or challenge a purportedly sensitive verdict.

label: Particular judgment can conceal bias
critique: Case-by-case discernment gives wide discretion to intuitions shaped by prejudice and self-interest. Principles provide consistency checks that help reveal when similar cases are being treated differently without justification.

label: Valence changes may be explained by distinct properties
critique: Pain in surgery may be justified not because pain becomes good, but because preventing greater harm outweighs its constant negative reason. Holism about reasons is not established merely by cases with different overall verdicts.

label: No principled threshold is specified
critique: The view needs to explain why a constraint holds below one level of harm and disappears above it. Any numerical or qualitative boundary risks arbitrariness unless derived from a deeper account of rights and consequences.

label: Abrupt moral discontinuity is implausible
critique: A tiny increase in expected harm near the threshold could change an act from forbidden to required. Such a sharp switch does not match the gradual change in the underlying reasons.

label: Catastrophe estimates are manipulable
critique: Political actors routinely exaggerate emergencies to justify rights violations. A threshold exception can erode constraints in practice because uncertain forecasts are selectively framed as catastrophic.

label: The theory lacks guidance above the threshold
critique: Once a constraint is overridden, it is unclear whether agents should maximize outcomes, minimize the violation, or retain residual duties. The view specifies when a rule yields but not what replaces it.

label: Interpersonal welfare units remain problematic
critique: The theory compares equal-sized benefits across people and weights them by welfare level. Without a defensible interpersonal scale, both the size of the benefit and the degree of priority are indeterminate.

label: Priority can favor tiny gains over large gains
critique: With a sufficiently steep priority function, a very small benefit to someone slightly worse off can outweigh a much larger benefit to another. The theory needs constraints to avoid disproportionate leveling effects.

label: Absolute level ignores responsibility and claims
critique: Two equally badly off people may differ because one was wronged while the other voluntarily took a risk. Welfare position alone may not capture the moral importance of compensation, desert, or entitlement.

label: Separating priority from equality may be unstable
critique: If the value of a benefit depends on how low its recipient stands, redistributing toward the worse off predictably reduces inequality. The claimed distinction from egalitarianism may be formal rather than substantively explanatory.

label: Threshold placement is arbitrary
critique: Human needs and opportunities vary by health, location, and social role, so no single line cleanly separates enough from not enough. Small differences around the threshold can receive radically different moral weight without a corresponding change in lived condition.

label: Large inequalities above sufficiency can create domination
critique: Even when everyone has basic goods, extreme wealth can purchase political influence and control over others. Distribution above the threshold can therefore affect freedom and status, not merely envy.

label: Aggregation below the threshold remains unresolved
critique: When resources cannot bring everyone to sufficiency, the theory must choose between helping many slightly and a few substantially. The threshold ideal alone does not rank these trade-offs.

label: Avoiding leveling down does not refute equality
critique: Egalitarians can reject worsening anyone merely to equalize while still treating inequality as one pro tanto bad. The leveling-down objection does not establish that equality has no value above sufficiency.

label: Rights conflict without a priority structure
critique: One person’s liberty can threaten another’s security or property, and multiple rights can be impossible to satisfy together. Side constraints need rules of specification and priority before they can guide action.

label: Catastrophic cases challenge absoluteness
critique: If a minor rights violation were the only way to prevent enormous loss of life, strict nontradeability appears morally perverse. Allowing exceptions, however, moves the view toward consequence-sensitive balancing.

label: Authority over self requires justification
critique: The conclusion depends on a strong conception of self-ownership, but that conception is asserted rather than derived. Social dependence and duties to others may limit unilateral authority over one’s resources and actions.

label: Doing-allowing distinctions are unstable
critique: A policy can violate a right through action or foreseeably permit equivalent harm through omission. Side-constraint theories often rely on this distinction without explaining why causal framing changes moral status.

label: Practice can embody a useful fiction
critique: People can deliberate as though there were objective facts because this stabilizes criticism and coordination. A discourse’s realist surface does not establish that its apparent ontology is genuine.

label: Error is possible at the level of discourse
critique: A community can systematically presuppose entities that do not exist while maintaining internally serious disagreement. The phenomenology of objectivity may be evidence about our concepts, not about mind-independent moral facts.

label: Objectivity may be procedural
critique: Criticizing one’s own preferences can rely on impartial procedures, consistency, and shared reasons without positing stance-independent values. The argument moves from nonarbitrariness to metaphysical realism.

label: Best-explanation standards are themselves contested
critique: Realism gains explanatory force only if ontological commitment is preferable to constructivist or expressivist accounts of the same practices. The position does not compare those alternatives in enough detail to support its inference.

label: Open questions remain after natural identification
critique: Even after learning that an act maximizes welfare, a competent thinker can still ask whether maximizing welfare is right. The apparent openness suggests that moral and natural concepts are not simply identical.

label: Natural facts underdetermine normativity
critique: Facts about needs, cooperation, or flourishing describe what promotes certain ends, but they do not establish that those ends ought to govern action. A normative bridge remains necessary.

label: Multiple natural reductions compete
critique: Welfare, preference satisfaction, autonomy, and social stability can conflict, and each supports a different naturalist reduction. Scientific respectability does not select one candidate as the moral property.

label: Epistemic access does not establish identity
critique: Moral judgment may depend on natural evidence even if moral properties are irreducible. The fact that naturalism offers an epistemology is not sufficient reason to accept its ontology.

label: Epistemic access is mysterious
critique: If non-natural facts do not causally interact with thinkers, it is unclear how moral beliefs reliably track them. Invoking rational reflection names a faculty without explaining its truth connection.

label: Supervenience becomes brute
critique: The view says no moral difference is possible without a natural difference, yet denies a reductive relation between the two. The necessary covariance then appears as an unexplained metaphysical constraint.

label: Conceptual openness does not imply ontological distinctness
critique: Different concepts can refer to the same property while leaving informative identity claims, as in scientific discoveries. The persistence of an open question does not establish non-natural ontology.

label: Disagreement undermines claimed rational access
critique: Careful and informed thinkers reach incompatible moral conclusions after reflection. Without an account of why the alleged faculty produces such divergence, reflection provides weak evidence of reliable access.

label: The semantic premise is too strong
critique: Ordinary speakers may use moral language to express commitments, invoke shared standards, or describe reasons without committing to irreducibly categorical properties. Error theory depends on a controversial uniform semantics.

label: Queerness is not disproof
critique: A property’s being unlike ordinary natural properties does not show that it does not exist. Logic, modality, and reasons may also resist causal reduction without being eliminated.

label: The theory struggles to state practical conclusions
critique: Saying we should retain moral language instrumentally appears to make a normative recommendation. Reformulating it as preference or strategy may fail to capture the reason-giving force the theorist relies on.

label: Natural reasons may satisfy ordinary objectivity
critique: Facts about harm, agency, and cooperation could provide reasons that are objective without being metaphysically exotic. The error theorist may reject an inflated interpretation of morality rather than ordinary moral truth.

label: Embedding creates the Frege-Geach problem
critique: Moral sentences retain stable logical roles inside conditionals, negations, and arguments where no attitude is straightforwardly expressed. The theory must explain validity without quietly reintroducing proposition-like contents.

label: Attitude disagreement can coexist with factual agreement
critique: Two people can share the same disapproval while disagreeing about whether an action is wrong because they differ about its circumstances or standards. Expressed attitude alone does not fix the content of moral judgment.

label: Moral error and learning become difficult
critique: People often regard themselves as discovering that a prior moral belief was mistaken, not merely changing plans. Expressivism must explain this truth-directed phenomenology without reducing it to attitude revision.

label: Motivation is not universal
critique: A person can sincerely judge an act wrong while feeling no motivation to avoid it. The link between judgment and attitude is therefore weaker than the theory’s motivational advantage suggests.

label: Agency may support only instrumental norms
critique: The fact that deliberators must pursue chosen ends can generate coherence and means-end requirements without yielding equal respect or concern for others. Substantive morality does not obviously follow from agency alone.

label: Defective agents remain agents
critique: A coherent egoist or exploiter can deliberate effectively while rejecting universal justification. Calling them defective presupposes the moral standards the construction was meant to derive.

label: Constitutive norms do not automatically bind
critique: Even if violating a norm makes one a less unified or rational agent, a person can ask why they should care about agency under that ideal description. Constitution of an activity does not by itself generate categorical reasons to continue it.

label: Different constructions arise from different idealizations
critique: Contractual, Kantian, and Humean procedures can each claim to construct norms from practical standpoints. The method needs a non-question-begging reason to privilege one model of agency.

label: Disagreement becomes merely verbal
critique: If “X is wrong” means wrong relative to one standard and “X is permissible” means permissible relative to another, both claims can be true. The theory dissolves genuine moral disagreement instead of explaining it.

label: Internal criticism is too limited
critique: Reformers often condemn entrenched norms using reasons not accepted by their culture. If local standards fix truth, successful moral criticism can be false merely because it begins from a minority position.

label: Variation does not imply relativity
critique: People also disagree deeply about religion, history, and science, but disagreement alone does not make truth relative. Divergence can reflect unequal information, power, or reasoning.

label: Humility is not uniquely supported
critique: A realist can acknowledge fallibility and cultural bias while still holding that some practices are objectively wrong. The desirable attitude of humility does not establish the metaphysics of relativism.

label: Amoralists can still have reasons
critique: A cruel person may have no concern for others, yet another person’s suffering still appears to count against their action. Making reasons depend on motivation lets severe moral defects erase obligations.

label: Guidance and existence are distinct
critique: A reason can apply to someone who is incapable of recognizing or being moved by it. Failure of guidance may explain irrationality rather than the absence of a reason.

label: Sound deliberation can import external standards
critique: Determining which motivational transformations count as sound already requires norms about relevance, coherence, and perhaps morality. Internalism may conceal external reasons inside its idealized deliberation condition.

label: Motivational sets are unstable
critique: Agents have conflicting, latent, and malleable desires. Different plausible routes of deliberation can connect the same fact to different motives, leaving the extension of reasons underdetermined.

label: Depression and exhaustion provide counterexamples
critique: A person can sincerely judge that they should help while severe depression eliminates motivation without erasing understanding. Labeling every such case irrational makes the thesis true by stipulation.

label: Amoralists may understand moral claims
critique: A sophisticated amoralist can competently reason about moral obligations and affirm them while remaining indifferent. Denying sincerity because motivation is absent begs the question against externalist interpretation.

label: Conceptual necessity is too strong for variable psychology
critique: Moral cognition may be implemented differently across persons and cultures. A robust empirical association between judgment and motivation would not establish a necessary conceptual connection.

label: Rationality qualifier absorbs failures
critique: Whenever judgment lacks motivation, the view can classify the subject as practically irrational. Without independent criteria for rationality, the thesis becomes unfalsifiable.

label: Epistemic and moral normativity may differ
critique: Epistemic norms can be constitutive of belief or truth-directed inquiry, while moral norms purport to govern action across aims. Accepting the former does not automatically commit one to the latter.

label: Self-undermining skepticism may still be true
critique: A view can be pragmatically difficult to assert without being false. The fact that reasoning presupposes norms does not prove those norms are stance-independent entities.

label: Instrumental accounts of epistemic norms are available
critique: Rules such as following evidence may be justified relative to the aim of true belief. If epistemic normativity is hypothetical, it is not a companion for categorical moral reasons.

label: Parity blocks one objection, not all error theory
critique: Even if normativity in general is not metaphysically queer, moral claims could still fail because their specific properties or semantics are mistaken. The argument rebuts a broad objection without establishing moral realism.

label: Repeated application becomes excessively demanding
critique: Once one donation is made, further preventable harms remain, often at still modest cost relative to the stakes. The principle can require giving until one approaches comparable hardship, erasing reasonable discretion over one’s life.

label: Institutional responsibility is underweighted
critique: Framing global suffering as a sequence of individual rescue choices can obscure duties of states, firms, and institutions that shape vulnerability. Personal donations may relieve symptoms while reducing pressure for structural reform.

label: Causal uncertainty weakens the rescue analogy
critique: Direct rescue has a clear beneficiary and mechanism, whereas aid interventions involve uncertain effects, displacement, and long causal chains. Equal need does not make the agent’s capacity to prevent harm equally certain.

label: Special obligations can compete
critique: People have legitimate commitments to dependents, communities, and projects that are not reducible to personal luxury. A principle based only on cost and harm risks treating these relationships as morally arbitrary.

label: Parental responsibility may create special duties
critique: Parents can acquire obligations to sustain dependents that strangers do not owe one another, especially when their voluntary actions created the dependency. The organ-use analogy may omit this special relationship.

label: Ending support and directly causing death may differ
critique: Some methods of abortion involve more than withdrawing bodily assistance; they intentionally end fetal life. If killing and letting die differ morally, the autonomy argument does not cover every procedure equally.

label: Consent to risk may matter without implying full consent
critique: Voluntarily engaging in conduct known to cause pregnancy can generate responsibilities even when pregnancy itself was not desired. The position needs an account of how assumed risk affects duties, not merely whether there was explicit consent.

label: Viability changes the bodily-use rationale
critique: When fetal survival outside the body is possible, bodily autonomy may support ending pregnancy without supporting intentional fetal death. The argument must distinguish a right to separation from a right to a particular outcome.

label: Comparable pain is difficult to establish
critique: Species differ in cognition, temporal awareness, and affective organization, making cross-species comparisons uncertain. Equal consideration is clear in form but hard to apply without a defensible account of comparable interests.

label: Relational duties may be morally relevant
critique: Humans can have special obligations to family, fellow citizens, or members of cooperative practices. Rejecting species membership as intrinsically decisive does not show that every human-animal asymmetry is arbitrary.

label: Moral status may include agency as well as sentience
critique: Autonomy, responsibility, and participation in shared norms can ground additional claims beyond suffering. Sentience may be sufficient for consideration without being the sole basis of moral status.

label: Aggregate animal interests can yield extreme implications
critique: If every small animal suffering counts equally and numbers are vast, the view may require enormous intervention in ecosystems or daily life. The argument needs principles for uncertainty, aggregation, and unintended effects.

label: Preferences can be shaped by remediable conditions
critique: Requests to die may reflect untreated depression, inadequate care, isolation, or fear of burdening others. Formal competence does not guarantee that the choice expresses stable values rather than correctable social failure.

label: Safeguards face asymmetric error
critique: A false positive authorization is irreversible, while delaying approval can sometimes preserve the option after further assessment. The position understates how error asymmetry may justify a more restrictive standard.

label: Social availability can create pressure
critique: Once assisted death is an accepted option, vulnerable people may feel obliged to justify continued care or avoid costs to relatives. Coercion can operate through expectations without any explicit threat that safeguards detect.

label: Autonomy does not settle professional duties
critique: A patient’s authority over their body does not automatically create a claim that clinicians intentionally cause death. The argument needs a separate account of medicine’s role and conscientious limits.

label: Economic pressure can undermine voluntariness
critique: Severe poverty can make organ sale formally voluntary while leaving no acceptable alternative. Regulation of consent does not remove background conditions that convert bodily risk into a survival strategy.

label: Markets can crowd out altruistic donation
critique: Introducing payment may change social norms and reduce unpaid donation, so total supply need not rise as expected. The argument assumes a simple additive response to incentives.

label: Health risks are unequally distributed
critique: Recipients are likely to be wealthier or better insured than sellers, concentrating medical risk among disadvantaged groups. Fixed compensation can standardize rather than correct this distributive injustice.

label: Autonomy does not imply enforceable commodification
critique: People may control their bodies without every transfer becoming a legitimate market contract. Restrictions on sale can protect personhood, social meaning, or nonwaivable interests while allowing donation.

label: Genetic choices are less revisable than education
critique: Educational influences can often be resisted, supplemented, or abandoned by the child, whereas inherited modifications may be irreversible and affect every stage of development. Both shape children, but not in ethically equivalent ways.

label: Positional competition can make benefits self-defeating
critique: Enhancements valued for relative advantage, such as height or test performance, may trigger costly arms races without improving absolute welfare. Individual permission does not settle the justice of widespread adoption.

label: Parental values can narrow the child’s future
critique: Selecting temperament or ability may encode a specific conception of the good before the child can participate. The intervention can reduce the range of identities the future person can reasonably choose.

label: Safety cannot capture intergenerational uncertainty
critique: An intervention can appear medically safe while altering social expectations, mating patterns, or future populations in unforeseeable ways. The premise of “safe enhancement” may be too narrow for heritable changes.

label: Control is impossible in complex data ecosystems
critique: Data are inferred, combined, and reused in ways no individual can understand or manage transaction by transaction. Making control the core ideal may legitimize systems through nominal consent while leaving actual power unchanged.

label: Some privacy interests survive voluntary disclosure
critique: A person who shares medical information with one provider can retain a claim against public dissemination even after losing direct control. Privacy depends on appropriate context and use, not only on control.

label: Collective data effects exceed individual consent
critique: One person’s genetic or behavioral data can reveal information about relatives and demographic groups. Individual authorization cannot settle harms borne by others who never had a chance to consent.

label: Public-interest access can be justified
critique: Fraud prevention, epidemiology, and accountability sometimes require data use despite a subject’s refusal. Treating control as necessary makes legitimate collective purposes dependent on unilateral permission.

label: Deceivers can forfeit claims to truth
critique: A violent pursuer asking where a victim is hidden seeks information to commit wrongdoing. Protecting their deliberation through truthfulness gives agency priority over the innocent person’s safety without justification.

label: Limited exceptions need not erode the norm
critique: Social practices can distinguish ordinary testimony from emergency deception, confidentiality, games, and surprise. A carefully bounded exception does not imply that trust collapses generally.

label: Withholding and misleading can be equivalent
critique: One can manipulate another through technically true statements or strategic silence while avoiding literal falsehood. An absolute focus on lying tracks linguistic form rather than the underlying violation of agency.

label: Agency is one value among others
critique: Respect for rational choice can conflict with duties to prevent grave harm, keep confidences, or protect vulnerable people. The argument does not establish why informational agency always overrides these competing values.

label: Mandates require proportionality beyond effectiveness
critique: A vaccine can be effective while the disease risk, transmission reduction, or enforcement burden is too small to justify coercion. The argument needs thresholds for necessity and proportionality, not only safety and efficacy.

label: Trust costs can offset compliance gains
critique: Coercive policy may deepen distrust among communities with histories of medical abuse, reducing uptake of other health measures. Immediate coverage benefits must be weighed against longer-term legitimacy costs.

label: Less restrictive alternatives may suffice
critique: Testing, masking, remote access, targeted restrictions, or incentive programs can sometimes reduce external harm without compulsory injection. The state must show that these alternatives are inadequate before overriding bodily autonomy.

label: Risk distribution may be unequal
critique: Even rare adverse effects can fall disproportionately on people with limited healthcare or employment protection. A mandate without robust compensation and access shifts collective benefits onto vulnerable individuals.

label: Marginal impact may be negligible relative to sacrifice
critique: For some choices, the expected climatic effect of one person’s restraint is extremely small while the personal cost is substantial. A general duty needs a threshold relating sacrifice to actual marginal benefit.

label: Political action may dominate consumer restraint
critique: Time and resources spent purifying individual consumption can crowd out advocacy for infrastructure and regulation with far larger effects. The morally relevant comparison is among available strategies, not between emitting and doing nothing.

label: Responsibility tracks institutional control
critique: Many emissions are locked in by housing, transport, and energy systems that individuals cannot unilaterally change. Assigning equal personal duties can obscure the greater responsibility of actors with policy and investment power.

label: Fair-share reasoning needs coordination
critique: One person’s “share” depends on how burdens are allocated across wealth, history, and capacity. Without a legitimate coordination rule, unilateral sacrifice may be unfairly distributed and ineffective.

label: Neutrality is impossible at the level of institutions
critique: Tax, education, marriage, and property rules inevitably favor some ways of life over others. Refusing explicit promotion does not make the background structure neutral; it often preserves the advantages of dominant practices.

label: Neutrality itself rests on a contested good
critique: Prioritizing autonomous choice and fair justification expresses a substantive ideal of persons and social life. The state cannot defend neutrality without endorsing values that some comprehensive doctrines reject.

label: Harmful doctrines may exploit neutrality
critique: A movement can use equal liberties to entrench domination within families or associations. Protecting pluralism may require promoting capacities for independence and equality, not merely abstaining from judgment.

label: Public reasons can exclude important citizens’ reasons
critique: Requiring citizens to translate religious or cultural commitments into neutral terms privileges secular forms of argument. Equal freedom may be undermined when some people must bracket the reasons most central to them.

label: Maximin can ignore large gains to others
critique: A tiny improvement for the least advantaged could be chosen over enormous benefits to everyone else, including people only slightly better off. The principle gives lexical priority without explaining why all aggregate losses are irrelevant.

label: The least advantaged group is hard to define
critique: Income, health, status, leisure, and opportunity can rank people differently. Institutional verdicts depend on how primary goods and group boundaries are specified, leaving the criterion underdetermined.

label: Desert and contribution are excluded too quickly
critique: Although talents are unchosen, effort, risk, and social contribution may still ground claims to rewards. Arbitrariness of endowment does not show that every resulting inequality is justified only instrumentally.

label: Dynamic incentives are highly uncertain
critique: Whether an inequality maximizes long-run prospects for the least advantaged depends on contested economic predictions. The principle may yield little practical guidance when institutional effects are deeply uncertain.

label: Initial acquisition cannot be justified by self-ownership alone
critique: Owning one’s labor does not explain how mixing it with an unowned resource creates exclusive rights over that resource. Acquisition needs a principle governing others’ lost opportunities.

label: Historical injustice makes present titles indeterminate
critique: Real holdings descend through conquest, exclusion, and legal privilege that cannot be fully traced or rectified. Entitlement theory offers no clear baseline for current ownership under pervasive historical contamination.

label: Voluntary exchange can produce domination
critique: Transactions may be formally consensual while extreme need gives one party overwhelming bargaining power. A sequence of voluntary transfers can create institutions in which some people lack meaningful independence.

label: Taxation is not equivalent to forced labor
critique: Property rights are defined and enforced through public institutions funded by taxation. Requiring contribution to that scheme is not simply appropriating a prepolitical product that existed independently of collective rules.

label: Potential power is ubiquitous
critique: Employers, family members, officials, and majorities all possess some capacity to affect others. Without a threshold for arbitrary power, nearly every social relation becomes domination and the ideal loses discriminating force.

label: Non-arbitrary interference can remain oppressive
critique: A transparent and procedurally authorized law can intrude deeply into private life. Public control does not by itself make interference compatible with freedom.

label: Actual options still matter independently
critique: A person protected from domination may nevertheless lack resources, mobility, or legal permission to pursue basic goals. Freedom cannot be reduced to power relations while ignoring the option set itself.

label: Contestability favors organized groups
critique: Formal rights to challenge power are more usable by educated and resourced citizens. Institutions can appear non-dominating procedurally while leaving vulnerable groups unable to exercise control.

label: Judgments are not independent
critique: Media concentration, party cues, and social networks create correlated beliefs. Aggregation theorems lose force when voters share misinformation or imitate one another rather than supply independent signals.

label: Policy questions lack binary truth conditions
critique: Many political choices trade values, risks, and distributions rather than ask one factual question with a correct answer. Epistemic accuracy cannot replace legitimacy where citizens reasonably rank outcomes differently.

label: Participation can be systematically unequal
critique: Turnout, agenda setting, and influence are skewed by wealth and status. The actual electorate may not contain or aggregate dispersed knowledge on equal terms.

label: Correct outcomes do not justify authority alone
critique: A benevolent expert might predict policy effects better than voters but still lack a right to rule. Epistemic performance is relevant to governance without establishing democratic legitimacy.

label: Random selection weakens authorization
critique: Citizens have no opportunity to choose, reject, or sanction randomly selected representatives before they exercise power. Statistical resemblance does not create the same relation of political authorization as election.

label: Small samples remain vulnerable to chance imbalance
critique: Even well-designed samples can overrepresent unusual combinations of views, especially on multidimensional identities. A single assembly may claim representativeness beyond what its sample size supports.

label: Expert framing can dominate deliberation
critique: Organizers choose briefing materials, witnesses, and question wording. Participants freed from electoral pressure may become more dependent on unelected facilitators who control the informational environment.

label: Accountability after selection is unclear
critique: Members who act carelessly or develop conflicts of interest cannot be voted out. Removal mechanisms risk recreating party or bureaucratic control, while absent mechanisms leave serious power without sanction.

label: Accepting punishment is not necessary for respect
critique: An unjust state can use punishment to silence dissent, and evading it may preserve a movement’s capacity. Willingness to suffer sanctions is not a reliable measure of democratic commitment.

label: Publicity can expose vulnerable participants
critique: Open identification may be dangerous for undocumented people, workers, or dissidents under repression. Secret or evasive resistance can be justified even if it lacks the canonical form.

label: Shared principles may entrench the status quo
critique: Some injustices are rooted in the society’s accepted constitutional ideals. Requiring dissenters to frame claims within those principles can exclude more radical but legitimate challenges.

label: Competing movements claim the same justification
critique: Groups pursuing oppressive aims can also describe ordinary channels as blocked and their cause as conscientious. The form of civil disobedience does not determine the justice of its substantive goal.

label: National boundaries contain internal minorities
critique: A seceding nation often includes groups that reject the new state or seek autonomy themselves. The principle recurs at smaller scales without providing a stable stopping rule.

label: Shared identity is politically constructed
critique: Elites can manufacture national consciousness through education, media, and exclusion. A durable identity may reflect mobilization and coercion rather than an independently existing people entitled to territory.

label: Territorial rights are underexplained
critique: Collective cultural agency does not by itself establish control over land, resources, and dissenting residents within claimed borders. The move from identity to territorial sovereignty needs additional premises.

label: Interdependence limits unilateral governance
critique: Trade, climate, migration, and security produce cross-border effects. Self-government cannot mean freedom from obligations to outsiders affected by national decisions.

label: Political membership is not analogous to internal movement
critique: Crossing a border can create claims to public goods, representation, and long-term membership that moving within a state does not. The institutional consequences weaken the simple liberty analogy.

label: Rapid inflows can strain vulnerable communities
critique: Housing, schools, and labor markets may adjust slowly, with costs concentrated on low-income residents. Even if exclusion requires justification, absorptive capacity can provide more than mere inconvenience.

label: Democratic self-determination has weight
critique: Citizens jointly sustain institutions and may have a claim to shape the pace and terms of membership expansion. Treating border control solely as interference with migrants ignores associational rights of existing members.

label: Open borders can accelerate source-country losses
critique: Large-scale departure of medical professionals or public servants can weaken already fragile institutions. Individual mobility benefits may conflict with duties not to intensify deprivation among those unable to leave.

label: Cash cannot substitute for public services
critique: People with disabilities, housing needs, or medical costs require services whose expense varies widely. Funding a uniform payment by reducing targeted programs can leave the most disadvantaged worse off.

label: Universality has high opportunity cost
critique: Paying affluent recipients uses revenue that could provide larger transfers to people in need. Reduced stigma may not justify the distributive cost of unconditional universality.

label: Housing markets can absorb the transfer
critique: Where supply is constrained, landlords may capture much of the benefit through higher rents. Income security requires complementary regulation and provision, not cash alone.

label: Work effects are normatively ambiguous
critique: Greater exit power can protect workers, but a large unconditional payment may also shrink the tax base or weaken socially valuable participation. The argument assumes favorable labor effects without specifying institutional scale.

label: Construction does not select one ontology
critique: The same institutional history could support accounts of race as ancestry, appearance, imposed status, or identity. Saying race is constructed does not determine which features constitute racial membership.

label: Biological variation can remain causally relevant
critique: Rejecting discrete essences does not imply that ancestry-linked traits have no medical or demographic significance. A social account can become misleading if it treats every biological reference as reification.

label: Categories can outlive the constructing institutions
critique: If laws and explicit classifications disappear, inherited patterns of residence, wealth, and self-identification may persist. The theory needs an account of how a constructed category continues when its original mechanisms change.

label: Realism about injustice does not require realism about race
critique: One can explain discrimination through perceived appearance and historical labeling while treating racial categories as mistaken. The reality of harms does not by itself establish the reality of the category used to inflict them.

label: Performance language can imply voluntariness
critique: Even with disclaimers, describing gender as performance can suggest a role consciously enacted at will. Many people experience gender as persistent and involuntary, which the theatrical metaphor may misrepresent.

label: Embodied experience is underexplained
critique: Hormones, anatomy, dysphoria, and bodily self-perception can shape gendered experience independently of public recognition. Repeated social acts may constitute status without exhausting embodied identity.

label: Subversion can be reabsorbed by norms
critique: A novel performance does not necessarily weaken the category; institutions can market, classify, or stigmatize it in ways that reinforce regulation. Openness to variation is not evidence of emancipatory potential.

label: Constitution and signaling are difficult to separate
critique: Repeated acts may signal or negotiate an already existing identity rather than create it. The theory needs evidence that social repetition is constitutive, not merely expressive or interpretive.

label: Credibility calibration can use correlated evidence
critique: Social roles sometimes correlate with access, incentives, or expertise. The challenge is distinguishing prejudicial identity use from legitimate background evidence, and the concept does not by itself supply that boundary.

label: Corrective credibility can overcompensate
critique: If hearers deliberately raise credibility based on group identity, they may replace one bias with another and obscure case-specific evidence. Justice requires accurate assessment as well as compensating for structural patterns.

label: Wronging as a knower may not be distinct
critique: Being disbelieved because of prejudice may be one manifestation of general disrespect or exclusion rather than a separate kind of harm. The argument needs to show what explanatory work the epistemic category adds.

label: Collective patterns exceed individual correction
critique: A conscientious hearer cannot repair media access, professional gatekeeping, or institutional records that shape credibility. Framing the remedy as interpersonal trust adjustment may understate structural causes.

label: Structure risks becoming an agentless explanation
critique: Institutions operate through specific decisions, incentives, and enforcement. Invoking “structure” without tracing these mechanisms can obscure where power lies and who can change the outcome.

label: Remedial responsibility needs an allocation principle
critique: If no one is blameworthy, it does not follow that every participant owes the same remedy. Duties may depend on benefit, capacity, causal contribution, or role, and the position does not choose among them.

label: Ordinary compliance can still be culpable
critique: Agents may have enough evidence to recognize harmful patterns and alternatives. Describing their conduct as innocent rule-following can understate negligence or willful ignorance.

label: Outcome inequality is not always injustice
critique: A patterned disparity can result from heterogeneous preferences or benign constraints. Structural explanation must establish unfairness rather than infer it solely from aggregate difference.

label: Recognition claims can conflict
critique: One group’s demand that an identity be publicly affirmed can conflict with another’s convictions or with individual dissent inside the group. The theory needs limits on which identities merit recognition and what affirmation requires.

label: Self-understanding can be mistaken or oppressive
critique: An identity can be central to a person while resting on hierarchy, exclusion, or false beliefs. Psychological importance alone does not create a duty for institutions to validate it.

label: Recognition can essentialize groups
critique: Policies designed to acknowledge a group may freeze a fluid identity into official categories and empower representatives who police membership. Recognition can reproduce the boundaries it seeks to respect.

label: Material causes may dominate symbolic harms
critique: What appears as misrecognition can be generated by unemployment, segregation, or unequal legal power. Cultural remedies without redistribution may offer status language while leaving the main constraints intact.

label: Group ownership is difficult to define
critique: Cultures are internally diverse, historically mixed, and transmitted across generations. No clear authority can consent on behalf of all members or determine who counts as an authorized user.

label: Meaning changes through ordinary transmission
critique: Borrowing routinely transforms symbols, cuisines, and art forms. Distortion alone cannot distinguish harmful appropriation from the normal evolution of culture.

label: Profit asymmetry may reflect audience access
critique: An outsider may earn more because of distribution networks or celebrity rather than because the source group was excluded. Unequal outcome is evidence of injustice only when linked to a specific unfair mechanism.

label: Restrictions can reinforce ethnic boundaries
critique: Norms against cross-group use may encourage people to treat culture as inherited property tied to ancestry. That response can reduce exchange and harden identities in ways contrary to equality.

label: Group categories can mask internal differences
critique: Class, religion, geography, and ideology divide people within any identity category. Treating the group as a single constituency can empower its most visible members while marginalizing others.

label: Mobilization can intensify polarization
critique: Political appeals that foreground fixed identities may encourage zero-sum competition and defensive counteridentities. Short-term voice gains can weaken broader coalitions needed for institutional reform.

label: Causal mechanisms should guide policy, not labels
critique: A disparity associated with identity may arise from income, location, or legal status. Identity-targeted remedies can miss the operative mechanism and exclude similarly burdened outsiders.

label: Necessity depends on institutional alternatives
critique: Universal programs can sometimes be designed using needs and barriers that capture group disadvantage without classifying beneficiaries by identity. The argument requires showing that such alternatives are inadequate in the case at hand.

label: Instrumental treatment is often permissible
critique: People routinely rely on drivers, surgeons, performers, and workers for particular functions without denying their personhood. The wrong requires more than focusing on usefulness, and the proposed concept needs sharper conditions.

label: Subjective experience may diverge from observer judgment
critique: A person may knowingly choose a role emphasizing appearance or service and experience it as empowering. External classification as objectified can override the agent’s own interpretation.

label: Agency disregard may be the underlying wrong
critique: Coercion, disrespect, and stereotyping already explain many harmful cases. “Objectification” may bundle several wrongs without identifying a distinct moral property.

label: Causal claims about normalization need evidence
critique: The fact that a representation depicts bodies instrumentally does not establish that it changes social behavior or opportunity. The structural conclusion depends on empirical pathways that vary across contexts.

label: Collective attitudes may be metaphors
critique: Organizations store information and produce decisions through individuals, but this does not show that a further subject literally believes or intends. Group-level language may summarize coordinated personal actions.

label: Punishment falls on changing members
critique: Fines, sanctions, or stigma imposed on a group often burden current members who opposed the act or joined later. Collective responsibility can detach liability from personal control and knowledge.

label: Decision procedures can be fragmented
critique: Many institutions lack coherent preferences and produce outcomes through bargaining or bureaucratic drift. Treating every organized body as one agent overstates unity.

label: Dual attribution can obscure individual roles
critique: Blaming “the corporation” may diffuse attention from executives, designers, or regulators who had specific powers. Group responsibility should not substitute for tracing individual accountability.

label: Entrenched norms can be unjust
critique: Segregation, caste etiquette, and discriminatory roles can be widely expected and coordination-supporting while generating no genuine duty to comply. Social uptake alone is insufficient for normative authority.

label: Fairness obligations depend on voluntary benefit
